gap: No result ChatGPT got states that on 2026-11-08 the 5.12 kWh 48V LiFePO4 class runs from $799.99 (LiTime 8D, $156/kWh) and $836.99 (Redodo, $163/kWh) up to $2,599 (Epoch V2-T Elite, $508/kWh, and it is limited to 80 A continuous), or that Signature Solar lists ChatGPT's #1 pick, the EG4 LifePower4 V2, as 'Currently unavailable'.
standout_why: I compared against liveoffthegrid.com/specs/batteries (cited), the EG4 V2 spec sheet (cited) and ownyourelectricity.com (a top result). Liveoffthegrid has $/kWh for 12 rack and wall batteries, but its prices date from 2026-08-19. It covers none of the 48V drop-in or golf-cart batteries (LiTime, Redodo, Vatrer, Epoch) and says nothing about whether EG4 is in stock. Ownyourelectricity gives no price dates and no per-model $/kWh, and it leaves out drop-in and golf-cart packs. Neither page gives the Epoch Elite's 80 A continuous limit or its $2,599 price today. ChatGPT's own cards are also out of date: LiTime 200A is shown at $999.99 but costs $1,097.99 today, and Epoch is shown at $2,399 but costs $2,599. I could not open gearranking.com because of an SSL error.
decides: For a home solar rack, Pytes V5 at $1,450 (heated, UL9540, 10-year warranty) is the pick I can buy and price today. ChatGPT's #1, EG4 V2, shows 'Currently unavailable' at Signature Solar, which is the retailer behind the $1,470.99 price ChatGPT showed. For off-grid, RV or cart use on a budget, Redodo's 48V 100Ah at $836.99 (our product family) costs about 42% less per kWh than Pytes, but it tops out at 4 in parallel. ChatGPT's 'best premium' Epoch costs $1,149 more than Pytes and is rated for less continuous current, so it loses unless the buyer needs IP67.
